title: Statistics - Lesson 5: Complementary Events Practice
description: Quick practice identifying complementary events and calculating complement probabilities.

questions.question: Which statement is the complement of "the selected student is present"?
options: The selected student is in Grade 10
The selected student is present and late
questions.explanation: The complement includes every outcome where the selected student is not present, so "absent" is the matching complement in this situation.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.46, what is P(not A)?
questions.explanation: Complement probabilities add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - 0.46 = 0.54.

questions.question: Complementary events cannot overlap.
questions.explanation: An outcome is either in event A or in not A. It cannot be in both at the same time.

questions.question: If 23 out of 50 learners passed a quiz, how many did not pass? Enter just the number.
questions.explanation: Use total minus the event count: 50 - 23 = 27 learners did not pass.

questions.question: The complement of "a score is greater than 80" is:
options: a score is less than or equal to 80
a score is equal to 80 only
questions.explanation: If a score is not greater than 80, it must be 80 or less. The boundary value 80 belongs in the complement.

questions.question: If P(rain) = 18%, what is P(no rain)?
questions.explanation: Use 100% - 18% = 82%. Rain and no rain are complements for the day described.

questions.question: If P(not B) = 0.31, what is P(B)? Enter a decimal.
In one or two sentences, explain why "likes volleyball" is not automatically the complement of "likes basketball."
questions.correctAnswer: They are not automatically complements because a student could like both sports, neither sport, or a different sport. The complement of likes basketball is does not like basketball.
questions.explanation: Complementary events must cover the whole sample space without overlap. Two different preferences may overlap or leave out other possibilities.
